summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct at the federal level. Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Section 377D's "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years. The federal territory of Kuala Lumpur stands directly under this Penal Code, with no local ordinance displacing it.

Every state and the federal territories also maintain Sharia enactments criminalising a man posing as a woman, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them; the federal Penal Code, however, applies to that visitor in full.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and conducted in public. On 28 November 2025 police together with Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) raided an all-male sauna in Chow Kit, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended.

The raid's aftermath carries direct exposure for foreign visitors. A magistrate rejected an extension of remand as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

The Human Dignity Trust records enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, alongside the 28 November operation. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that Jawi had his full licence to carry out enforcement against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences intact, and a High Court had earlier refused to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021 including residents of Kuala Lumpur, describe state-sponsored discrimination as a defining feature of daily life and call on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical picture is one of raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but venue-based operations now reach into the capital's nightlife and bath venues without warning, and detainees' identities can be published before any charge is laid.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch reports regression in the climate for LGBT people as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground, quoting a Kuala Lumpur activist on the direction of policy. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, which means the decriminalisation the same report urges is not a near-term change a visitor can plan around.

The pattern of exposure is collective rather than individual: the Chow Kit operation targeted a venue, produced 208 arrests in one night, and was followed within a week by a second raid in Penang. Media pre-notification and the publication of detainees' personal details mean the reputational harm of an arrest can precede any judicial finding.

The narrowing of Sharia provisions by the Federal Court on federalism grounds in 2021 and 2024 should not be read as a general liberalising trend. Those judgments removed state competence over the provisions; they left the federal Penal Code offences fully intact and did not decriminalise same-sex conduct anywhere in Malaysia.

Compared with jurisdictions where gender nonconformity is policed through ordinary criminal law alone, Malaysia layers a federal sodomy regime on top of sub-national Sharia offences enforced by dedicated religious departments, with a documented history of corporal punishment as a sentence.
localsOnly:
Cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" remain criminal under Sharia enactments in all 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, and enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments. Three states also bar women from posing as men. The laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

The Religious Affairs Minister's July 2020 statement granting Jawi his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons remains an operative statement of official policy; the International Commission of Jurists called for it to be revoked. Residents of the capital face the direct consequence of that posture in stop-and-search activity around religious-department operations.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law, so employment, housing and service refusals based on gender expression have no statutory remedy. Seventeen civil servants identified in the 28 November 2025 raid were suspended from their posts.

Killing of transgender women has recurred with official indifference: three trans women were killed in fewer than two months before 25 June 2019, and documentation of the Klang case records police mistreatment and impunity. The documented case file's own heading for that account is "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".
outOfScopeNotes:
The immigration consequences for the 31 foreign nationals detained on 28 November 2025, including whether any faced removal, visa cancellation or an entry ban, are not stated in the available sources and remain unresolved. Embassy intervention is documented; the outcome is not.

Whether any of the 208 detainees were ultimately charged under section 377B, and the disposition of the cases after the magistrate's refusal of the remand extension, is not sourced here. The Home Minister's 2 December remark about revisiting the provisions was a floated position, not tabled legislation.

The status of the constitutional challenge pending as of late 2014, filed after the arrest of 16 trans women on 8 June 2014, is not resolved in the available material. So too, the Human Rights Watch material is dated 10 August 2022 and rests on interviews conducted between 2018 and 2021, so conditions after that reporting window are evidenced only by the 2024 and 2025 items above.

Section 377D is listed in the federal profile but is not named in connection with the 28 November 2025 operation; the charges recorded for that raid are under section 377B. Whether section 377D is used in other venue operations is not sourced.
